Question: So firstly, tell us a bit about yourself.  Where do you live?
Answer: I'm Olivia, I'm in my mid 50s now, I live in Yarrabrook, out on Coorindal Station Track—so yes, I’m very country Victoria. I’m about as far from Melbourne as you can get, tucked right near the corner where NSW, SA, and Victoria meet, right along the banks of the fictional Coorindal River

Question: what's your migraine like, tell me about your migraine.
Answer: OK, I've had migraines since I was 13.  So I have had them for a very long time and I had migraine 24/7.  So if I was lucky I would have a couple of hours off from having a migraine every month.  So I was had them all the time.  I was at the stage where I pretty much was getting asked all the time at work.  When was I looking at retiring.  I, yeah, could not function.  I come from a family of migraine sufferers from both sides of my family.  Both my mother and my paternal grandfather were migraine sufferers.  I have a sister that's a migraine sufferer as well.  So it's it, it's just there.  Two of my children also have my migraines as well.

Question: So how long you have migraine?  Like how many years were you all day, every day?
Answer: Probably from my mid 20s onwards. So 20 plus years, yeah, that's a pretty long slog. So I'm proud of myself for still being here, if I can say that as gently as I can, because one of the things that we are always concerned about as a community is that you get to a point where the relentlessness of it just gets too much.  So there is actually a day in Migraine Awareness Month, it's called Shine a Light Day on June 7, where we acknowledge people who have died because of migraine.  It's started by charity in the US.  It's never been done here, but we're going to include it in the schedule for this year anyway.

Question: Let's get back and talk about more positive things.  So I'm presuming you tried absolutely everything else before Aimovig.
Answer: I did.  I'm actually very lucky that I have a very supportive GP.  He's his wife also suffered from migraines so it's his ex-wife now.  But every time that he came across something that was new he would trial it on both her and me at the same time.  We're actually really close friends.  We're actually in the same theatre group together and we've known each other since the mid 80s.  And yeah, so he would, as soon as he found out on something about something that he could prescribe, he would try on both of us to see if it worked.  And then if it didn't work, he'd go, okay, now I've got to find something else.  So he would, we went, we did eye drops, we did anything that he could possibly think of.  He would try it on me to see if it would work.  Sometimes it would work on, it would work for a short time and then it wouldn't work anymore and he'd be getting really frustrated with the fact that that it wouldn't work.  So I'm very lucky that way that he would try anything he possibly could.  And then it got to the point where, yeah, it was OK.  I mean, I need to see a neurologist like because he just couldn't find anything that he could do that he himself could do anymore, that it had to be a neurologist that did it then.

Question: So you got referred off to a neuro?
Answer: I did reffered to neurologist.

Question: Have neurologist tried Botox route for the treatment of Migraine before Aimovig?
Answer: Yes, I did Botox for several years.  In the meantime, though, I did have a cerebral Hemangioma rupture, so I had to have surgery to remove that.  And that was misdiagnosed by our local hospital as just another migraine.  So my doctor went that is not just another migraine.  And he was the one that discovered that I had a severe rupture and got me sent to see neurosurgeon.  And so, yeah, in between that and was my neurologist, that's when we had a lot more other things happening too.

Question: So your brains not happy, You've tried everything.  You've had one of the the complications that we have, unhappy brains have?
Answer: Two brain aneurysms. Stroke.  Imagine, Homer.  Yeah.  OK, we have to laugh about it, right?  It's a bit of dark humor.  Yeah.  Migraine brains are very unhappy brains, and they do kind of present more commonly, particularly with aneurysms and strokes.  I do take it seriously,  If it doesn't feel like a normal attack, don't let a doctor tell me that it is just a migraine attack.  I get it checked out.  At least get an MRI if I live somewhere you do have MRI, which is not always the case.

Question: So, all right, how did you go with Aimovig?
Answer: Aimovig was absolutely wonderful.  I started taking it in January 2019 and immediately, almost immediately, within a week and a half, the migraine stopped, stopped, stopped.

Question: So Migraine stopped with Aimovig. Like somebody turned off a switch?
Answer: Absolutely.  And when they're thinking this, this is just got to be like, this can't be real.

Question: What's going on, your Migraine disappered with Aimovig, can you explain in detail like what happened when you had your first shot of Aimovig?
Answer: Yeah, this can't be right.  I've got, I've got to be getting another like what?  What on earth is happening?  And I think it was about four months later, I got my first migraine, which was all of three hours.  And I went, 'cause I'm there thinking, yeah, if one's gotta happen, it's gotta happen.  And when it actually when I was A and it was only a day or two before the injection was due.  And I'm going, OK, I'm about, I'm running out.  So that's obviously why I'm getting this little thing.  That's because I'm due to have my injection.  And I think in that whole 15 months I had, I did have one big migraine, which I ended up in hospital for, ended up in the Emergency department for a whole 72 hours.  And I was counting, but it was a hemoplagic 1.  And so I, they were worried that I was having a stroke.  I mean, I knew it wasn't a stroke because I've had the stroke symptoms before.  It wasn't the same as when I did have it, but they were very concerned.  So they kept me in the emergency department for for 72 hours.  But other than that one, I think I had about maybe 3 breakthroughs on the day or the day before that I was meant to have the injection and they were only a couple of hours.

Question: Can you share someone else Aimovig experience (family or friend) you know?
Answer: A friend of mine went through something very similar. Initially, their migraines were pretty intense—daily for years. But after starting Aimovig treatment, they saw a dramatic shift. Within six weeks, they went from having migraines every single day to having more migraine-free days than not. It was like someone flipped a switch. They described it as a phenomenal feeling—like suddenly being themselves again. It took about six months to reach zero migraine days, and they stayed that way for a year until they stopped the treatment. Interestingly, they also mentioned that the anxiety actually increased at first, especially anticipating the next big attack. It took time and therapy to work through that and to allow themselves to feel well without fear.

Question: With Aimovig, How did you find that transition from completely debilitated to I'm good?
Answer: Yeah, I kept waiting for like it was a case of when, when's it going to hit?  When when is this thing going to be?  Yeah, I kept expecting something bad to happen the whole time I'm expecting something bad.  And I mean, when I did have that bad one, I'm going, Yep, Yep, this makes sense.  It's going to be there.  But then it just took longer and longer.  I thought it was right.  It said that whole it's. The anticipation, the fear of the next attack is actually worse than the attack.  So I kind of come out of that phase and.  And I had, you know, a good year of pretty good life, really.

Question: What led to the decision to come off Aimovig?
Answer: Pretty much we couldn't afford it.  I only work part time because I'm a part time teacher and I have this, at that point, I had a child at university who is solely funded because we earn that little bit too much from government, according to them, for them to be able to give him any money.  And yes, so and I've got another child that's at home who has a mental illness.  So we are looking, we look after him.  So yeah, we basically could not afford it.  So I had been transferred to something that was slightly more affordable so.

Question: So when you came off Aimovig, did you have a gap between coming off Aimovig and starting Emgality?
Answer: I didn't, I went back from one to the other.  I have ended up I've I've got a lot of complications with Emgality.  I've ended up with severe food allergies, but I can put up with that if I can put up with not being able to have coffee, gluten, lactose.

Question: Does Emgality  make life harder though for you?
Answer: I mean, I'm, I'm, it makes life, it makes life very hard, but I can, I can put up with it if it means that I can still have most days migraine free.  I don't know.  I don't have.  I still get migraines on it.  I've had three this month. That's so it's not nearly as good as a Aimovig, and I'll go back to a Aimovig in an absolute heartbeat if we could afford it. And if it if it was at the same price, yeah, that would be there would be no questions asked.

Question: Have you friend/family tried switching migraine treatments to Emgality? What was there experience like for you, did it help or make things worse?
Answer: A friend of mine had a really tough experience when they tried switching treatments. They took six weeks off and then tried Emgality, but it didn’t help at all—in fact, things got worse. They described it as a rapid decline back into migraine hell. Just a couple of weeks after missing their first Aimovig shot, they had a massive hemiplegic migraine—couldn’t walk, sit up, eat, or drink. Emgality felt like a placebo to them, and they even experienced mood swings and weight gain. Eventually, they went back to Aimovig and started over. The improvement was quick, but not as complete as before—still a few breakthrough attacks and lingering aura-like symptoms. It was a tough journey, but they’re slowly getting back on track.

Question: Did you get any warning signs or premonitory symptoms even after starting Aimovig treatment? How do they compare to what you used to experience?
Answer: I still experiences some premonitory symptoms—like feeling a bit off, sometimes euphoric, or getting tingling sensations and visual auras. But the difference now is that most of these symptoms don’t lead to full-blown attacks anymore. Occasionally, a few still do, but compared to where they were—completely debilitated, unable to walk, sit up, or even feed themselves—it’s a massive improvement. They often say people don’t realize how life-changing this shift is, especially when the treatment that makes it possible isn’t covered by the government, even though it costs around $264 a month.

Question: Do you feel like access to effective migraine treatment has impacted your ability to live independently or contribute to society? What’s your take on how Aimovig treatment costs are handled?
Answer: I would like to make powerful point about the cost of migraine treatment. I still experience some premonitory symptoms—like tingling, visual auras, or even brief euphoric feelings—but the difference now is huge. They’ve gone from being completely debilitated—unable to walk, sit up, or even feed themselves—to functioning again. And what’s frustrating is that this transformation comes from a treatment that costs just $264 a month. They couldn’t understand why anyone would deny that—why keep someone in a state of disability, unable to work or contribute, when the solution is so accessible? It’s not just about health—it’s about dignity, independence, and being allowed to live a full life.

Anyway, let's go back to talking about the drugs from the politics, because I'll get too cranky.
Answer: I was going to say, what was I found really interesting was when I was in hospital for those three days, one of the doctors and not for their doctors, one of the Med students who pretends that they're a doctor that was in the emergency department.  I had said that I was on Amovig and myself this time they look at me and they go, what?  She said, oh, I've had my sister's on that good.  And then when she said and what, where's your pain?  And I said, ah, it said about 5 to 6.  She said, oh, so an 8 to 9 for any normal person.  Yeah, I thought she knows. So I thought that was really nice actually having someone that relates to someone that has migraine and knew exactly where we actually stood because when they when they say, well where's your pain level?  Our pain levels are something completely different to anyone else's pain levels.

Question: But anyway, what advice, just to wrap this up, would you give to somebody who is either thinking about trying Aimovig or is on Aimovig and thinking about switching to Emgality?
Answer: Look for me, the reason to go with the Emgality was for start, my GP could prescribe it and I didn't have to keep going down to the neurologist, which for me is 3 to 4 days off work.  So I would say if, if you could remain on Amovig and you didn't have to worry about the taking days off work and things like that, absolutely stick to Amovig.  If money was not a worry, stick to a Amovig.  I, I hope that the government gets off their **** and just doesn't please, please understand we really need this.  It's like a Amovig.  I said if I if I could go, if I could afford to go back on it, I would.

Question: Is there any side effects on Aimovig at all?
Answer: Oh, a bit of dropping of hair.  But I had masses and masses of hair, so a little bit of dropping meant nothing.
